As John prepared Christ's way, so Christ prepared his own, and made way for the further discoveries he designed, with the doctrine of repentance. <hi type="italic">If any man</hi> will do this part of <hi type="italic">his will, he shall know</hi> more of <hi type="italic">his doctrine,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. [2.] This is preached <hi type="italic">often</hi> upon; wherever he went, this was his subject, and neither he nor his followers ever reckoned it worn threadbare, as those would have done, that have <hi type="italic">itching ears,</hi> and are fond of novelty and variety more than that which is truly edifying. Note, That which has been preached and heard before, may yet very profitably be preached and heard again; but then it should be preached and heard better, and with new affections; what Paul had said before, he said again, <hi type="italic">weeping,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.18">18</reference>. [3.] This he preached as gospel; "Repent, review your ways, and return to yourselves." Note, The doctrine of repentance is right gospel-doctrine. Not only the austere Baptist, who was looked upon as a melancholy, morose man, but the sweet and gracious Jesus, whose lips dropped as a honey-comb, preached repentance; for it is an unspeakable privilege that room is left for repentance. [4.] The reason is still the same; The <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven is at hand;</hi> for it was not reckoned to be fully come, till that pouring out of the Spirit after Christ's ascension. John had preached the kingdom of heaven at hand above a year before this; but now it was so much the stronger; now is the <hi type="italic">salvation nearer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Rom. xiii. 11</reference>. We should be so much the more quickened to our duty, <hi type="italic">as we see the day approaching,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">Heb. x. 25</reference>.
entries.de8a07e7072e94ef1065641ef78548060aee8f95: <div eID="gen21406" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Calls Peter, Andrew, James, and John.</title> <div sID="gen21407" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. <hi type="super">20</hi> And they straightway left <hi type="italic">their</hi> nets, and followed him. 21 And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James <hi type="italic">the son</hi> of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. 22 And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him. <div eID="gen21407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21408" type="x-p"/> When Christ began to preach, he began to <hi type="italic">gather disciples,</hi> who should now be the <hi type="italic">hearers,</hi> and hereafter the <hi type="italic">preachers,</hi> of his doctrine, who should now be witnesses <hi type="italic">of</hi> his miracles, and hereafter <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> them. Now, in these verses, we have an account of the first disciples that he called into fellowship with himself. <div eID="gen21408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21409" type="x-p"/> And this was an instance, 1. Of <hi type="italic">effectual calling</hi> to Christ. In all his preaching he gave a common call to all the country, but in this he gave a special and particular call to those that were given him by the Father. Let us see and admire the power of Christ's grace, own his word to be the rod of his strength, and wait upon him for those powerful influences which are necessary to the efficacy of the gospel call—those distinguishing influences. All the country was <hi type="italic">called,</hi> but these were <hi type="italic">called out,</hi> were <hi type="italic">redeemed from among them.</hi> Christ was so manifested to them, as he was not manifested unto the world. 2. It was an instance of <hi type="italic">ordination,</hi> and appointment to the work of the ministry. When Christ, as a Teacher, set up his great school, one of his first works was to appoint ushers, or under masters, to be employed in the work of instruction. Now he began to give gifts unto men, to put the treasure into earthen vessels. It was an early instance of his care for the church. <div eID="gen21409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21410" type="x-p"/> Now we may observe here, <div eID="gen21410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21411" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">Where</hi> they were called—by the <hi type="italic">sea of Galilee,</hi> where Jesus was walking, Capernaum being situated near that sea. Concerning this sea of Tiberias, the Jews have a saying, That of all the seven seas that God made, he made choice of none but the sea of Gennesaret; which is very applicable to Christ's choice of it, to honour it, as he often did, with his presence and his miracles. Here, on the banks of the sea, Christ was walking for contemplation, as Isaac in the field; hither he went to call his disciples; not to Herod's court (for few mighty or noble are called), not to Jerusalem, among the chief priests and the elders, but to the sea of Galilee; surely Christ sees not as man sees. Not but that the same power which effectually called Peter and Andrew would have wrought upon Annas and Caiaphas, for with God nothing is impossible; but, as in other things, so in his converse and attendance, he would humble himself, and show that God ha <hi type="italic">chosen the poor of this world.</hi> Galilee was a remote part of the nation, the inhabitants were less cultivated and refined, their very language was broad and uncouth to the curious, their <hi type="italic">speech betrayed them.</hi> They who were picked up at the sea of Galilee, had not the advantages and improvements, no, not of the more polished Galileans; yet thither Christ went, to call his apostles that were to be the prime ministers of state in his kingdom, for he <hi type="italic">chooses the foolish things of this world, to confound the wise.</hi> <div eID="gen21411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21412" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">Who</hi> they were. We have an account of the call of two pair of brothers in these verses—Peter and Andrew, James and John; the two former, and, probably, the two latter also, had had acquaintance with Christ before (<reference osisRef="John.1.40-John.1.41">John i. 40, 41</reference>), but were not till now called into a close and constant attendance upon him. Note, Christ brings poor souls by degrees into fellowship with himself. They had been disciples of John, and so were the better disposed to follow Christ. Note, Those who have submitted to the discipline of repentance, shall be welcome to the joys of faith. We may observe concerning them, <div eID="gen21412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21413" type="x-p"/> 1. That they were <hi type="italic">brothers.</hi> Note, It is a blessed thing, when they who are <hi type="italic">kinsmen according to the flesh</hi> (as the apostle speaks, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.3">Rom. ix. 3</reference>), are brought together into a spiritual alliance to Jesus Christ. It is the honour and comfort of a house, when those that are of the <hi type="italic">same</hi> family, are of <hi type="italic">God's</hi> family. <div eID="gen21413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21414" type="x-p"/> 2. That they were <hi type="italic">fishers.</hi> Being fishers, (1.) They were <hi type="italic">poor men:</hi> if they had had estates, or any considerable stock in trade, they would not have made fishing their trade, however, they might have made it their recreation. Note, Christ does not despise the poor, and therefore we must not; the poor are evangelized, and the Fountain of honour sometimes gives more abundant honour to that part which most lacked. (2.) The were <hi type="italic">unlearned men,</hi> not bred up to books or literature as Moses was, who was conversant with all the learning of the Egyptians. Note, Christ sometimes chooses to endow those with the gifts of grace who have least to show of the gifts of nature. Yet this will not justify the bold intrusion of ignorant and unqualified men into the work of the ministry: extraordinary gifts of knowledge and utterance are not now to be expected, but requisite abilities must be obtained in an ordinary way, and without a competent measure of these, none are to be admitted to that service. (3.) They were <hi type="italic">men of business,</hi> who had been bred up to labour. Note, Diligence in an honest calling is pleasing to Christ, and no hindrance to a holy life. Moses was called from keeping sheep, and David from following the ewes, to eminent employments. Idle people lie more open to the temptations of Satan than to the calls of God. (4.) They were men that were accustomed to <hi type="italic">hardships</hi> and hazards; the fisher's trade, more than any other, is laborious and perilous; fishermen must be often wet and cold; they must watch, and wait, and toil, and be often in <hi type="italic">perils by waters.</hi> Note, Those who have learned to bear hardships, and run hazards, are best prepared for the fellowship and discipleship of Jesus Christ. Good soldiers of Christ must endure hardness. <div eID="gen21414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21415" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">What they were doing.</hi> Peter and Andrew were then using their nets, they were fishing; and James and John were <hi type="italic">mending their nets,</hi> which was an instance of their industry and good husbandry. They did not go to their father for money to buy new nets, but took pains to mend their old ones. It is commendable to make what we have go as far, and last as long, as may be. James and John were <hi type="italic">with their father Zebedee,</hi> ready to assist him, and make his business easy to him. Note, It is a happy and hopeful presage, to see children careful of their parents, and dutiful to them. Observe, 1. They were <hi type="italic">all</hi> employed, all very busy, and none idle. Note, When Christ comes, it is good to be found doing. "Am I in Christ?" is a very needful question for us to ask ourselves; and, next to that, "Am I in my calling?" 2. They were <hi type="italic">differently</hi> employed; two of them were fishing, and two of them <hi type="italic">mending their nets.</hi> Note, Ministers should be always employed, either in teaching or studying; they may always find themselves something to do, if it be not their own fault; and <hi type="italic">mending their nets,</hi> is, in its season, as necessary work as fishing. <div eID="gen21415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21416" type="x-p"/> IV. <hi type="italic">What the call was</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.</hi> They had followed Christ before, as ordinary disciples (<reference osisRef="John.1.37">John i. 37</reference>), but so they might follow Christ, and follow their calling too; therefore they were called to a more close and constant attendance, and must leave their calling. Note, Even they who had been called to follow Christ, have need to be called to follow on, and to follow nearer, especially when they are designed for the work of the ministry. Observe, <div eID="gen21416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21417" type="x-p"/> 1. What Christ intended them for; <hi type="italic">I will make you fishers of men;</hi> this alludes to their former calling. Let them be not proud of the new honour designed them, they are still but fishers; let them not be afraid of the new work cut out for them, for they have been used to fishing, and fishers they are still. It was usual with Christ to speak of spiritual and heavenly things under such allusions, and in such expressions, as took rise from common things that offered themselves to his view. David was called from feeding sheep to feed God's Israel; and when he is a king, is a shepherd. Note, (1.) Ministers are <hi type="italic">fishers of men,</hi> not to destroy them, but to save them, by bringing them into another element. They must fish, not for wrath, wealth, honour, and preferment, to gain them to themselves, but for souls, to gain them to Christ. <hi type="italic">They watch for your souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">Heb. xiii. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">and seek not yours, but you,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2 Cor. xii. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">16</reference>. (2.) It is Jesus Christ that makes them so; <hi type="italic">I will make you fishers of men.</hi> It is he that qualifies men for this work, calls them to it, authorizes them in it, gives them commission to fish for souls, and wisdom to win them. Those ministers are likely to have comfort in their work, who are thus made by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen21417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21418" type="x-p"/> 2. What they must do in order to this; <hi type="italic">Follow me.</hi> They must separate themselves to a diligent attendance on him, and set themselves to a humble imitation of him; must follow him as their Leader. Note, (1.) Those whom Christ employs in any service for him, must first be fitted and qualified for it. (2.) Those who would <hi type="italic">preach Christ,</hi> must first <hi type="italic">learn</hi> Christ, and learn of him. How can we expect to bring others to the knowledge of Christ, if we do not know him well ourselves? (3.) Those who would get an acquaintance with Christ, must be diligent and constant in their attendance on him. The apostles were prepared for their work, by <hi type="italic">accompanying Christ all the time that he went in and out among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.21">Acts i. 21</reference>. There is no learning comparable to that which is got by following Christ. Joshua, by ministering to Moses, is fitted to be his successor. (4.) Those who are to fish for men, must therein follow Christ, and do it as he did, with diligence, faithfulness, and tenderness. Christ is the great pattern for preachers, and they ought to be <hi type="italic">workers together with him.</hi> <div eID="gen21418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21419" type="x-p"/> V. What was the <hi type="italic">success</hi> of this call. Peter and Andrew <hi type="italic">straightway left their nets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.20">v. 20</reference>); and James and John <hi type="italic">immediately left the ship and their father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.22">v. 22</reference>); <hi type="italic">and they</hi> all <hi type="italic">followed him.</hi> Note, Those who would follow Christ aright, must <hi type="italic">leave all</hi> to follow him. Every Christian must leave all in affection, set loose to all, must <hi type="italic">hate father and mother</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>), must love them less than Christ, must be ready to part with his interest in them rather than with his interest in Jesus Christ; but those who are devoted to the work of the ministry are, in a special manner, concerned to disentangle themselves from all the affairs of this life, that they may give themselves wholly to that work which requires the whole man. Now, <div eID="gen21419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21420" type="x-p"/> 1. This instance of the power of the Lord Jesus gives us good encouragement to depend upon the sufficiency of his grace. How strong and effectual is his word! <hi type="italic">He speaks, and it is done.</hi> The same power goes along with this word of Christ, <hi type="italic">Follow me,</hi> that went along with that word, <hi type="italic">Lazarus, come forth;</hi> a power <hi type="italic">to make willing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen21420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21421" type="x-p"/> 2. This instance of the pliableness of the disciples, gives us a good example of obedience to the command of Christ. Note, It is the good property of all Christ's faithful servants to come when they are called, and to follow their Master wherever he leads them. They objected not their present employments, their engagements to their families, the difficulties of the service they were called to, or their own unfitness for it; but, being called, they obeyed, and, like Abraham, <hi type="italic">went out not knowing whither they went,</hi> but knowing very well whom they followed. James and John <hi type="italic">left their father:</hi> it is not said what became of him; their mother Salome was a constant follower of Christ; no doubt, their father Zebedee was a believer, but the call to follow Christ fastened on the young ones. Youth is the learning age, and the labouring age. The priests ministered in the prime of their life.
entries.203fa5024b1a06d3821fa765281eac42f7e309e0: <div eID="gen21421" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Preaches in Galilee; Miracles of Christ in Galilee.</title> <div sID="gen21422" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people. <hi type="super">24</hi> And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatic, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them. <hi type="super">25</hi> And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> Decapolis, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> Jerusalem, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> Judea, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> beyond Jordan. <div eID="gen21422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21423" type="x-p"/> See here, I. What an industrious preacher Christ was; He <hi type="italic">went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom.</hi> Observe, 1. <hi type="italic">What</hi> Christ preached—<hi type="italic">the gospel of the kingdom. The kingdom of heaven,</hi> that is, of grace and glory, is emphatically <hi type="italic">the kingdom, the kingdom</hi> that was now to come; that kingdom which shall survive, as it doth surpass, all the kingdoms of the earth. <hi type="italic">The gospel</hi> is the charter of that kingdom, containing the King's coronation oath, by which he has graciously obliged himself to pardon, protect, and save the subjects of that kingdom; it contains also their oath of allegiance, by which they oblige themselves to observe his statutes and seek his honour; this is <hi type="italic">the gospel of the kingdom;</hi> this Christ was himself the Preacher of, that our faith in it might be confirmed. 2. <hi type="italic">Where</hi> he preached—<hi type="italic">in the synagogues;</hi> not there only, but there chiefly, because those were <hi type="italic">the places of concourse,</hi> where <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> was to <hi type="italic">lift up her voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 21</reference>); because they were <hi type="italic">places of concourse</hi> for religious worship, and there, it was to be hoped, the minds of the people would be prepared to receive <hi type="italic">the gospel;</hi> and there the scriptures of the Old Testament were read, the exposition of which would easily introduce <hi type="italic">the gospel of the kingdom.</hi> 3. <hi type="italic">What pains he took</hi> in preaching; He <hi type="italic">went about all Galilee, teaching.</hi> He might have issued out a proclamation to summon all to come to him; but, to show his humility, and the condescensions of his grace, he goes to them; for he <hi type="italic">waits to be gracious,</hi> and comes <hi type="italic">to seek and save.</hi> Josephus says, There were above two hundred cities and towns in Galilee, and all, or most of them, Christ visited. He <hi type="italic">went about doing good.</hi> Never was there such an itinerant preacher, such an indefatigable one, as Christ was; he went from town to town, to beseech poor sinners to be reconciled to God. This is an example to ministers, to lay themselves out to do good, and to <hi type="italic">be instant,</hi> and constant, in <hi type="italic">season, and out of season,</hi> to preach the word. <div eID="gen21423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21424" type="x-p"/> II. What a powerful physician Christ was; he <hi type="italic">went about</hi> not only <hi type="italic">teaching,</hi> but <hi type="italic">healing,</hi> and both with his word, that he might magnify that above all his name. <hi type="italic">He sent his word, and healed them.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen21424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21425" type="x-p"/> 1. What diseases he cured—all without exception. He <hi type="italic">healed all manner of sickness, and all manner of disease.</hi> There are diseases which are called <hi type="italic">the reproach of physicians,</hi> being obstinate to all the methods they can prescribe; but even those were the glory of this Physician, for <hi type="italic">he healed them</hi> all, however inveterate. His word was the true <hi type="italic">panpharmacon—all-heal.</hi> <div eID="gen21425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21426" type="x-p"/> Three general words are here used to intimate this; he healed every sickness, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">noson</hi></hi>, as blindness, lameness, fever, dropsy; every <hi type="italic">disease,</hi> or languishing, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">malakian</hi></hi>, as fluxes and consumptions; and all <hi type="italic">torments,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">basanous</hi></hi>, as gout, stone, convulsions, and such like torturing distempers; whether the disease was acute or chronical; whether it was a racking or a wasting disease; none was too bad, none too hard, for Christ to heal with a word's speaking. <div eID="gen21426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21427" type="x-p"/> Three particular diseases are specified; <hi type="italic">the palsy,</hi> which is the greatest weakness of the body; <hi type="italic">lunacy,</hi> which is the greatest malady of the mind, and <hi type="italic">possession of the Devil,</hi> which is the greatest misery and calamity of both, yet Christ healed all: for he is the sovereign Physician both of soul and body, and has command of all diseases. <div eID="gen21427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21428" type="x-p"/> 2. What patients he had. A physician who was so easy of access, so sure of success, who cured immediately, without either a painful suspense and expectation, or such painful remedies as are worse than the disease; who cured gratis, and took no fees, could not but have abundance of patients. See here, what flocking there was to him from all parts; great multitudes of people came, not only <hi type="italic">from Galilee</hi> and the country about, but even <hi type="italic">from Jerusalem</hi> and <hi type="italic">from Judea,</hi> which lay a great way off; for <hi type="italic">his fame went throughout all Syria,</hi> not only among all the people of the Jews, but among the neighbouring nations, which, by the report that now spread far and near concerning him, would be prepared to receive his gospel, when afterwards it should be brought them. <hi type="italic">This</hi> is given as the reason why such multitudes came to him, because his fame had spread so widely. Note, What we hear of Christ from others, should invite us to him. The queen of Sheba was induced, by the fame of Solomon, to pay him a visit. The voice of fame is "Come, and see." Christ both <hi type="italic">taught and healed.</hi> They who came for cures, met with instruction concerning <hi type="italic">the things that belonged to their peace.</hi> It is well if any thing will bring people to Christ; and they who come to him will find more in him than they expected. These Syrians, like Naaman the Syrian, coming to be healed of their diseases, many of them being converts, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.15">2 Kings v. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.17">17</reference>. They sought health for the body, and obtained the salvation of the soul; like Saul, who sought the asses, and found the kingdom. Yet it appeared, by the issue, that many of those who rejoiced in Christ as a Healer, forgot him as a Teacher. <div eID="gen21428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21429" type="x-p"/> Now concerning the cures which Christ wrought, let us, once for all, observe the <hi type="italic">miracle,</hi> the <hi type="italic">mercy,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mystery,</hi> of them. <div eID="gen21429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21430" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">miracle</hi> of them. They were wrought in such a manner, as plainly spake them to be the immediate products of a divine and supernatural power, and they were God's seal to his commission. Nature could not do these things, it was the God of nature; the cures were many, of diseases incurable by the art of the physician, of persons that were strangers, of all ages and conditions; the cures were wrought openly, before many witnesses, in mixed companies of persons that would have denied the matter of fact, if they could have had any colour for so doing; no cure ever failed, or was afterwards called in question; they were wrought speedily, and not (as cures by natural causes) gradually; they were perfect cures, and wrought with a word's speaking; all which proves him <hi type="italic">a Teacher come from God,</hi> for, otherwise, none could have done the works that he did, <reference osisRef="John.3.2">John iii. 2</reference>. He appeals to these as credentials, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.4-Matt.11.5">ch. xi. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.36">John v. 36</reference>. It was expected that the Messiah should work miracles (<reference osisRef="John.7.31">John vii. 31</reference>); miracles of this nature (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6">Isa. xxxv. 5, 6</reference>); and we have this indisputable proof of his being the Messiah; never was there any man that did thus; and therefore his healing and his preaching generally went together, for the former confirmed the latter; thus here he <hi type="italic">began to</hi> do <hi type="italic">and to</hi> teach, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.1">Acts i. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen21430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21431" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> of them. The miracles that Moses wrought, to prove his mission, were most of them plagues and judgments, to intimate the terror of that dispensation, though from God; but the miracles that Christ wrought, were most of them cures, and all of them (except the cursing of the barren fig tree) blessings and favours; for the gospel dispensation is founded, and built up in love, and grace, and sweetness; and the management is such as tends not to affright but to allure us to obedience. Christ designed by his cures to win upon people, and to ingratiate himself and his doctrine into their minds, and so to draw them with the bands of love, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Hos. xi. 4</reference>. The miracle of them proved his doctrine <hi type="italic">a faithful saying,</hi> and convinced men's judgments; the mercy of them proved it <hi type="italic">worthy of all acceptation,</hi> and wrought upon their affections. They were not only <hi type="italic">great</hi> works, but <hi type="italic">good works,</hi> that he <hi type="italic">showed them from</hi> his <hi type="italic">Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.32">John x. 32</reference>); and this goodness was intended to <hi type="italic">lead men to repentance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Rom. ii. 4</reference>), as also to show that kindness, and beneficence, and doing good to all, to the utmost of our power and opportunity, are essential branches of that holy religion which Christ came into the world to establish. <div eID="gen21431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21432" type="x-p"/> (3.) The <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> of them. Christ, by curing <hi type="italic">bodily diseases,</hi> intended to show, that his great errand into the world was to cure <hi type="italic">spiritual maladies.</hi> He is the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness,</hi> that <hi type="italic">arises with</hi> this <hi type="italic">healing under his wings.</hi> As the Converter of sinners, he is the <hi type="italic">Physician of souls,</hi> and has taught us to call him so, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.12-Matt.9.13">ch. ix. 12, 13</reference>. Sin is the <hi type="italic">sickness, disease,</hi> and <hi type="italic">torment</hi> of the soul; Christ <hi type="italic">came to take away sin,</hi> and so to heal these. And the particular stories of the cures Christ wrought, may not only be applied spiritually, by way of allusion and illustration, but, I believe, are very much intended to reveal to us spiritual things, and to set before us the way and method of Christ's dealing with souls, in their conversion and sanctification; and those cures are recorded, that were most significant and instructive this way; and they are therefore so to be explained and improved, to the honour and praise of that glorious Redeemer, <hi type="italic">who forgiveth all our iniquities, and</hi> so <hi type="italic">healeth all our diseases.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.4"/> <div eID="gen21432" type="x-p"/>

entries.eaec70c96da4fbe05f16bc7728f140692316d716: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13326"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11">Mt 4:1-11</reference>. Temptation of Christ. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.1.12">Mr 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.1-Luke.4.13">Lu 4:1-13</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13326"/><hi type="bold">1. Then--</hi>an indefinite note of sequence. But Mark's word (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.12">Mr 1:12</reference>) fixes what we should have presumed was meant, that it was "immediately" after His baptism; and with this agrees the statement of Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.1">Lu 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen25333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was Jesus led up--</hi>that is, from the low Jordan valley to some more elevated spot.<div eID="gen25334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the Spirit--</hi>that blessed Spirit immediately before spoken of as descending upon Him at His baptism, and abiding upon Him. Luke, connecting these two scenes, as if the one were but the sequel of the other, says, "Jesus, being full of the Holy Ghost, returned from Jordan, and was led," &c. Mark's expression has a startling sharpness about it--"Immediately the Spirit driveth Him" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.12">Mr 1:12</reference>), "putteth," or "hurrieth Him forth," or "impelleth Him." (See the same word in <reference osisRef="Mark.1.43">Mr 1:43</reference>; 5:40; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.25">Mt 9:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.52">13:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.4">Joh 10:4</reference>). The thought thus strongly expressed is the mighty constraining impulse of the Spirit under which He went; while Matthew's more gentle expression, "was led up," intimates how purely voluntary on His own part this action was.<div eID="gen25335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the wilderness--</hi>probably the wild Judean desert. The particular spot which tradition has fixed upon has hence got the name of Quarantana or Quarantaria, from the forty days--"an almost perpendicular wall of rock twelve or fifteen hundred feet above the plain" [Robinson, Palestine]. The supposition of those who incline to place the temptation amongst the mountains of Moab is, we think, very improbable.<div eID="gen25336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be tempted--</hi>The Greek word (peirazein) means simply to try or make proof of; and when ascribed to God in His dealings with men, it means, and can mean no more than this. Thus, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.1">Ge 22:1</reference>, "It came to pass that God did tempt Abraham," or put his faith to a severe proof. (See <reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">De 8:2</reference>). But for the most part in Scripture the word is used in a bad sense, and means to entice, solicit, or provoke to sin. Hence the name here given to the wicked one--"the tempter" (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.3">Mt 4:3</reference>). Accordingly "to be tempted" here is to be understood both ways. The Spirit conducted Him into the wilderness simply to have His faith tried; but as the agent in this trial was to be the wicked one, whose whole object would be to seduce Him from His allegiance to God, it was a temptation in the bad sense of the term. The unworthy inference which some would draw from this is energetically repelled by an apostle (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13-Jas.1.17">Jas 1:13-17</reference>).<div eID="gen25337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the devil--</hi>The word signifies a slanderer--one who casts imputations upon another. Hence that other name given him (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Re 12:10</reference>), "The accuser of the brethren, who accuseth them before our God day and night." Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.13">Mr 1:13</reference>) says, "He was forty days tempted of Satan," a word signifying an adversary, one who lies in wait for, or sets himself in opposition to another. These and other names of the same fallen spirit point to different features in his character or operations. What was the high design of this? First, as we judge, to give our Lord a taste of what lay before Him in the work He had undertaken; next, to make trial of the glorious equipment for it which He had just received; further, to give Him encouragement, by the victory now to be won, to go forward spoiling principalities and powers, until at length He should make a show of them openly, triumphing over them in His cross: that the tempter, too, might get a taste, at the very outset, of the new kind of material in man which he would find he had here to deal with; finally, that He might acquire experimental ability "to succor them that are tempted" (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.18">He 2:18</reference>). The temptation evidently embraced two stages: the one continuing throughout the forty days' fast; the other, at the conclusion of that period.<div eID="gen25338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25339" type="x-p"/> First Stage: <div eID="gen25339" type="x-p"/>
entries.815b791e89c4fedcd4e8c0df4f3be3edee215213: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13327"/><div sID="gen25340" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13327"/><hi type="bold">2. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights--</hi>Luke says "When they were quite ended" (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.2">Lu 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen25340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25341" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he was afterward an hungered--</hi>evidently implying that the sensation of hunger was unfelt during all the forty days; coming on only at their close. So it was apparently with Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.28">Ex 34:28</reference>) and Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.8">1Ki 19:8</reference>) for the same period. A supernatural power of endurance was of course imparted to the body, but this probably operated through a natural law--the absorption of the Redeemer's Spirit in the dread conflict with the tempter. (See on <reference osisRef="Acts.9.9">Ac 9:9</reference>). Had we only this Gospel, we should suppose the temptation did not begin till after this. But it is clear, from Mark's statement, that "He was in the wilderness forty days tempted of Satan" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.13">Mr 1:13</reference>), and Luke's, "being forty days tempted of the devil" (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.2">Lu 4:2</reference>), that there was a forty days' temptation before the three specific temptations afterwards recorded. And this is what we have called the First Stage. What the precise nature and object of the forty days' temptation were is not recorded. But two things seem plain enough. First, the tempter had utterly failed of his object, else it had not been renewed; and the terms in which he opens his second attack imply as much. But further, the tempter's whole object during the forty days evidently was to get Him to distrust the heavenly testimony borne to Him at His baptism as THE Son of God--to persuade Him to regard it as but a splendid illusion--and, generally, to dislodge from His breast the consciousness of His Sonship. With what plausibility the events of His previous history from the beginning would be urged upon Him in support of this temptation it is easy to imagine. And it makes much in support of this view of the forty days' temptation that the particulars of it are not recorded; for how the details of such a purely internal struggle could be recorded it is hard to see. If this be correct, how naturally does the Second Stage of the temptation open! In Mark's brief notice of the temptation there is one expressive particular not given either by Matthew or by Luke--that "He was with the wild beasts" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.12">Mr 1:12</reference>), no doubt to add terror to solitude, and aggravate the horrors of the whole scene. <div eID="gen25341" type="x-p"/>
entries.88f30a75fd9e66d9ef35b640d03e7af3a07e647c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13328"/><div sID="gen25342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13328"/><hi type="bold">3. And when the tempter came to him--</hi>Evidently we have here a new scene.<div eID="gen25342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he said, if thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread--</hi>rather, "loaves," answering to "stones" in the plural; whereas Luke, having said, "Command this stone," in the singular, adds, "that it be made bread," in the singular (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.3">Lu 4:3</reference>). The sensation of hunger, unfelt during all the forty days, seems now to have come on in all its keenness--no doubt to open a door to the tempter, of which he is not slow to avail himself; "Thou still clingest to that vainglorious confidence that Thou art the Son of God, carried away by those illusory scenes at the Jordan. Thou wast born in a stable; but Thou art the Son of God! hurried off to Egypt for fear of Herod's wrath; but Thou art the Son of God! a carpenter's roof supplied Thee with a home, and in the obscurity of a despicable town of Galilee Thou hast spent thirty years, yet still Thou art the Son of God! and a voice from heaven, it seems, proclaimed it in Thine ears at the Jordan! Be it so; but after that, surely Thy days of obscurity and trial should have an end. Why linger for weeks in this desert, wandering among the wild beasts and craggy rocks, unhonored, unattended, unpitied, ready to starve for want of the necessaries of life? Is this befitting "the Son of God?" At the bidding of "the Son of God" surely those stones shall all be turned into loaves, and in a moment present an abundant repast." <div eID="gen25343" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d52f829e1987a87f6929ddd9564da60601aa6d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13329"/><div sID="gen25344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13329"/><hi type="bold">4. But he answered and said, It is written--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.8.3">De 8:3</reference>).<div eID="gen25344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Man shall not live by bread alone--</hi>more emphatically, as in the Greek, "Not by bread alone shall man live."<div eID="gen25345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God--</hi>Of all passages in Old Testament Scripture, none could have been pitched upon more apposite, perhaps not one so apposite, to our Lord's purpose. "The Lord ... led thee (said Moses to Israel, at the close of their journeyings) these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep His commandments, or no. And He humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that He might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only," &c., "Now, if Israel spent, not forty days, but forty years in a waste, howling wilderness, where there were no means of human subsistence, not starving, but divinely provided for, on purpose to prove to every age that human support depends not upon bread, but upon God's unfailing word of promise and pledge of all needful providential care, am I, distrusting this word of God, and despairing of relief, to take the law into My own hand? True, the Son of God is able enough to turn stones into bread: but what the Son of God is able to do is not the present question, but what is man's duty under want of the necessaries of life. And as Israel's condition in the wilderness did not justify their unbelieving murmurings and frequent desperation, so neither would Mine warrant the exercise of the power of the Son of God in snatching despairingly at unwarranted relief. As man, therefore, I will await divine supply, nothing doubting that at the fitting time it will arrive." The second temptation in this Gospel is in Luke's the third. That Matthew's order is the right one will appear, we think, quite clearly in the sequel. <div eID="gen25346" type="x-p"/>
entries.289cd3da313ea7edf5ee4781c4a4252fd1955317: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13330"/><div sID="gen25347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13330"/><hi type="bold">5. Then the devil taketh him up--</hi>rather, "conducteth Him."<div eID="gen25347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the holy city--</hi>so called (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.2">Is 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.1">Ne 11:1</reference>) from its being "the city of the Great King," the seat of the temple, the metropolis of all Jewish worship.<div eID="gen25348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple--</hi>rather, "the pinnacle"--a certain well-known projection. Whether this refers to the highest summit of the temple, which bristled with golden spikes [Josephus, Antiquities, 5.5,6]; or whether it refers to another peak, on Herod's royal portico, overhanging the ravine of Kedron, at the valley of Hinnom--an immense tower built on the very edge of this precipice, from the top of which dizzy height Josephus says one could not look to the bottom [Antiquities, 15.11,5]--is not certain; but the latter is probably meant. <div eID="gen25349" type="x-p"/>
entries.6545f3ca2ac6874041109f88ccb36f10804b3f90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13331"/><div sID="gen25350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13331"/><hi type="bold">6. And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God--</hi>As this temptation starts with the same point as the first--our Lord's determination not to be disputed out of His Sonship--it seems to us clear that the one came directly after the other; and as the remaining temptation shows that the hope of carrying that point was abandoned, and all was staked upon a desperate venture, we think that remaining temptation is thus shown to be the last; as will appear still more when we come to it.<div eID="gen25350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast thyself down--</hi>"from hence" (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.9">Lu 4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen25351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for it is written--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.91.11">Psa 91:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.12">12</reference>). "But what is this I see?" exclaims stately Bishop Hall. "Satan himself with a Bible under his arm and a text in his mouth!" Doubtless the tempter, having felt the power of God's Word in the former temptation, was eager to try the effect of it from his own mouth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.14">2Co 11:14</reference>).<div eID="gen25352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands--</hi>rather, "on their hands."<div eID="gen25353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone--</hi>The quotation is, precisely as it stands in the Hebrew and the Septuagint, save that after the first clause the words, "to keep thee in all thy ways," are here omitted. Not a few good expositors have thought that this omission was intentional, to conceal the fact that this would not have been one of "His ways," that is, of duty. But as our Lord's reply makes no allusion to this, but seizes on the great principle involved in the promise quoted, so when we look at the promise itself, it is plain that the sense of it is precisely the same whether the clause in question be inserted or not. <div eID="gen25354" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb4081010c7ab19a3cacff3be2f0715643acb38d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13332"/><div sID="gen25355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13332"/><hi type="bold">7. Jesus said unto him, It is written again--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.6.16">De 6:16</reference>), as if he should say, "True, it is so written, and on that promise I implicitly rely; but in using it there is another Scripture which must not be forgotten."<div eID="gen25355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God--</hi>"Preservation in danger is divinely pledged: shall I then create danger, either to put the promised security skeptically to the proof, or wantonly to demand a display of it? That were 'to tempt the Lord my God,' which, being expressly forbidden, would forfeit the right to expect preservation." <div eID="gen25356" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c02a474c2da06f7ce924883867cfc638f60ad1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13333"/><div sID="gen25357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13333"/><hi type="bold">8. Again, the devil taketh him up--</hi>"conducteth him," as before.<div eID="gen25357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into--</hi>or "unto"<div eID="gen25358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an exceeding high mountain, and showeth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.5">Lu 4:5</reference>) adds the important clause, "in a moment of time"; a clause which seems to furnish a key to the true meaning. That a scene was presented to our Lord's natural eye seems plainly expressed. But to limit this to the most extensive scene which the natural eye could take in, is to give a sense to the expression, "all the kingdoms of the world," quite violent. It remains, then, to gather from the expression, "in a moment of time"--which manifestly is intended to intimate some supernatural operation--that it was permitted to the tempter to extend preternaturally for a moment our Lord's range of vision, and throw a "glory" or glitter over the scene of vision: a thing not inconsistent with the analogy of other scriptural statements regarding the permitted operations of the wicked one. In this case, the "exceeding height" of the "mountain" from which this sight was beheld would favor the effect to be produced. <div eID="gen25359" type="x-p"/>
entries.57138a08417b6642ad57bcb6fbfdd525a0b860e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13334"/><div sID="gen25360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13334"/><hi type="bold">9. And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee--</hi>"and the glory of them," adds Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.6">Lu 4:6</reference>). But Matthew having already said that this was "showed Him," did not need to repeat it here. Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.6">Lu 4:6</reference>) adds these other very important clauses, here omitted--"for that is," or "has been," "delivered unto me, and to whomsoever I will I give it." Was this wholly false? That were not like Satan's unusual policy, which is to insinuate his lies under cover of some truth. What truth, then, is there here? We answer, Is not Satan thrice called by our Lord Himself, "the prince of this world" (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.30">14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.11">16:11</reference>)? Does not the apostle call him "the god of this world" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>)? And still further, is it not said that Christ came to destroy by His death "him that hath the power of death, that is, the devil" (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>)? No doubt these passages only express men's voluntary subjection to the rule of the wicked one while they live, and his power to surround death to them, when it comes, with all the terrors of the wages of sin. But as this is a real and terrible sway, so all Scripture represents men as righteously sold under it. In this sense he speaks what is not devoid of truth, when he says, "All this is delivered unto me." But how does he deliver this "to whomsoever he will?" As employing whomsoever he pleases of his willing subjects in keeping men under his power. In this case his offer to our Lord was that of a deputed supremacy commensurate with his own, though as his gift and for his ends.<div eID="gen25360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if thou wilt fall down and worship me--</hi>This was the sole but monstrous condition. No Scripture, it will be observed, is quoted now, because none could be found to support so blasphemous a claim. In fact, he has ceased now to present his temptations under the mask of piety, and he stands out unblushingly as the rival of God Himself in his claims on the homage of men. Despairing of success as an angel of light, he throws off all disguise, and with a splendid bribe solicits divine honor. This again shows that we are now at the last of the temptations, and that Matthew's order is the true one. <div eID="gen25361" type="x-p"/>
entries.f26440e82c78a95453bd6b540bc11f2eb4d0a426: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13335"/><div sID="gen25362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13335"/><hi type="bold">10. Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan--</hi>Since the tempter has now thrown off the mask, and stands forth in his true character, our Lord no longer deals with him as a pretended friend and pious counsellor, but calls him by his right name--His knowledge of which from the outset He had carefully concealed till now--and orders him off. This is the final and conclusive evidence, as we think, that Matthew's must be the right order of the temptations. For who can well conceive of the tempter's returning to the assault after this, in the pious character again, and hoping still to dislodge the consciousness of His Sonship, while our Lord must in that case be supposed to quote Scripture to one He had called the devil to his face--thus throwing His pearls before worse than swine?<div eID="gen25362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for it is written--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">De 6:13</reference>). Thus does our Lord part with Satan on the rock of Scripture.<div eID="gen25363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou shalt worship--</hi>In the Hebrew and the Septuagint it is, "Thou shalt fear"; but as the sense is the same, so "worship" is here used to show emphatically that what the tempter claimed was precisely what God had forbidden.<div eID="gen25364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve--</hi>The word "serve" in the second clause, is one never used by the Septuagint of any but religious service; and in this sense exclusively is it used in the New Testament, as we find it here. Once more the word "only," in the second clause--not expressed in the Hebrew and the Septuagint--is here added to bring out emphatically the negative and prohibitory feature of the command. (See <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Ga 3:10</reference> for a similar supplement of the word "all" in a quotation from <reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">De 27:26</reference>). <div eID="gen25365" type="x-p"/>
entries.489bf9318aec3494dcfe3f9e7d18bfeeb3fabaf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13336"/><div sID="gen25366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13336"/><hi type="bold">11. Then the devil leaveth him--</hi>Luke says, "And when the devil had exhausted"--or "quite ended," as in <reference osisRef="Luke.4.2">Lu 4:2</reference>--"every (mode of) temptation, he departed from him till a season." The definite "season" here indicated is expressly referred to by our Lord in <reference osisRef="John.14.30">Joh 14:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="Luke.22.52">Lu 22:52</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.53">53</reference>.<div eID="gen25366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him--</hi>or supplied Him with food, as the same expression means in <reference osisRef="Mark.1.31">Mr 1:31</reference> and <reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Lu 8:3</reference>. Thus did angels to Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.5-1Kgs.19.8">1Ki 19:5-8</reference>). Excellent critics think that they ministered, not food only, but supernatural support and cheer also. But this would be the natural effect rather than the direct object of the visit, which was plainly what we have expressed. And after having refused to claim the illegitimate ministration of angels in His behalf, oh, with what deep joy would He accept their services when sent, unasked, at the close of all this temptation, direct from Him whom He had so gloriously honored! What "angels' food" would this repast be to Him! and as He partook of it, might not a Voice from heaven be heard again, by any who could read the Father's mind, "Said I not well, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased?"<div eID="gen25367" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.4.12-Matt.4.25">Mt 4:12-25</reference>. Christ Begins His Galilean Ministry--Calling of Peter and Andrew, James and John--His First Galilean Circuit. ( = Mr 1:14-20, 35-39; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.14">Lu 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.15">15</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">There is here a notable gap in the history, which but for the fourth Gospel we should never have discovered. From the former Gospels we should have been apt to draw three inferences, which from the fourth one we know to be erroneous: First, that our Lord awaited the close of John's ministry, by his arrest and imprisonment, before beginning His own; next, that there was but a brief interval between the baptism of our Lord and the imprisonment of John; and further, that our Lord not only opened His work in Galilee, but never ministered out of it, and never visited Jerusalem at all nor kept a passover till He went thither to become "our Passover, sacrificed for us." The fourth Gospel alone gives the true succession of events; not only recording those important openings of our Lord's public work which preceded the Baptist's imprisonment--</hi>extending to the end of the third chapter--but so specifying the passover which occurred during our Lord's ministry as to enable us to line off, with a large measure of certainty, the events of the first three Gospels according to the successive passovers which they embraced. Eusebius, the ecclesiastical historian, who, early in the fourth century, gave much attention to this subject, in noticing these features of the Evangelical Records, says [Ecclesiastical History, 3.24] that John wrote his Gospel at the entreaty of those who knew the important materials he possessed, and filled up what is wanting in the first three Gospels. Why it was reserved for the fourth Gospel, published at so late a period, to supply such important particulars in the life of Christ, it is not easy to conjecture with any probability. It may be, that though not unacquainted with the general facts, they were not furnished with reliable details. But one thing may be affirmed with tolerable certainty, that as our Lord's teaching at Jerusalem was of a depth and grandeur scarcely so well adapted to the prevailing character of the first three Gospels, but altogether congenial to the fourth; and as the bare mention of the successive passovers, without any account of the transactions and discourses they gave rise to, would have served little purpose in the first three Gospels, there may have been no way of preserving the unity and consistency of each Gospel, so as to furnish by means of them all the precious information we get from them, save by the plan on which they are actually constructed.<div eID="gen25368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25369" type="x-p"/> Entry into Galilee (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.12-Matt.4.17">Mt 4:12-17</reference>). <div eID="gen25369" type="x-p"/>
entries.915c41e7e88e1a8f3e48b3daa754bbeb9b9c6246: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13337"/><div sID="gen25370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13337"/><hi type="bold">12. Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison--</hi>more simply, "was delivered up," as recorded in <reference osisRef="Matt.14.3-Matt.14.5">Mt 14:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.17-Mark.6.20">Mr 6:17-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.19">Lu 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.20">20</reference>.<div eID="gen25370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he departed--</hi>rather, "withdrew."<div eID="gen25371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into Galilee--</hi>as recorded, in its proper place, in <reference osisRef="John.4.1-John.4.3">Joh 4:1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen25372" type="x-p"/>
entries.53dbd308fc06be50d8c0bbe58c3895a8761bb480: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13338"/><div sID="gen25373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13338"/><hi type="bold">13. And leaving Nazareth--</hi>The prevalent opinion is that this refers to a first visit to Nazareth after His baptism, whose details are given by Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.16">Lu 4:16</reference>, &c.); a second visit being that detailed by our Evangelist (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.54-Matt.13.58">Mt 13:54-58</reference>), and by Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.1-Mark.6.6">Mr 6:1-6</reference>). But to us there seem all but insuperable difficulties in the supposition of two visits to Nazareth after His baptism; and on the grounds stated in <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16">Lu 4:16</reference>, &c., we think that the one only visit to Nazareth is that recorded by Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.53-Matt.13.58">Mt 13:53-58</reference>), Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.1-Mark.6.6">Mr 6:1-6</reference>), and Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.14-Luke.4.30">Lu 4:14-30</reference>). But how, in that case, are we to take the word "leaving Nazareth" here? We answer, just as the same word is used in <reference osisRef="Acts.21.3">Ac 21:3</reference>, "Now when we had sighted Cyprus, and left it on the left, we sailed into Syria,"--that is, without entering Cyprus at all, but merely "sighting" it, as the nautical phrase is, they steered southeast of it, leaving it on the northwest. So here, what we understand the Evangelist to say is, that Jesus, on His return to Galilee, did not, as might have been expected, make Nazareth the place of His stated residence, but, "leaving [or passing by] Nazareth,"<div eID="gen25373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the seacoast--</hi>maritime Capernaum, on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee; but the precise spot is unknown. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.11.23">Mt 11:23</reference>). Our Lord seems to have chosen it for several reasons. Four or five of the Twelve lived there; it had a considerable and mixed population, securing some freedom from that intense bigotry which even to this day characterizes all places where Jews in large numbers dwell nearly alone; it was centrical, so that not only on the approach of the annual festivals did large numbers pass through it or near it, but on any occasion multitudes could easily be collected about it; and for crossing and recrossing the lake, which our Lord had so often occasion to do, no place could be more convenient. But one other high reason for the choice of Capernaum remains to be mentioned, the only one specified by our Evangelist.<div eID="gen25374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim--</hi>the one lying to the west of the Sea of Galilee, the other to the north of it; but the precise boundaries cannot now be traced out. <div eID="gen25375" type="x-p"/>
entries.37436b0abc1c4cd8383ce19595c44909999a8d33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13339"/><div sID="gen25376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13339"/><hi type="bold">14. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Is 9:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">2</reference> or, as in Hebrew, Isaiah 8:23, and 9:1).<div eID="gen25376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying--</hi>as follows: <div eID="gen25377" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ad5af49ece9b2b3e525477b9ad61366ec8e911f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13340"/><div sID="gen25378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13340"/><hi type="bold">15. The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea--</hi>the coast skirting the Sea of Galilee westward--beyond Jordan--a phrase commonly meaning eastward of Jordan; but here and in several places it means westward of the Jordan. The word seems to have got the general meaning of "the other side"; the nature of the case determining which side that was.<div eID="gen25378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Galilee of the Gentiles--</hi>so called from its position, which made it the frontier between the Holy Land and the external world. While Ephraim and Judah, as Stanley says, were separated from the world by the Jordan valley on one side and the hostile Philistines on another, the northern tribes were in the direct highway of all the invaders from the north, in unbroken communication with the promiscuous races who have always occupied the heights of Lebanon, and in close and peaceful alliance with the most commercial nation of the ancient world, the Phoenicians. Twenty of the cities of Galilee were actually annexed by Solomon to the adjacent kingdom of Tyre, and formed, with their territory, the "boundary" or "offscouring" (Gebul or Cabul) of the two dominions--at a later time still known by the general name of "the boundaries (coasts or borders) of Tyre and Sidon." In the first great transportation of the Jewish population, Naphtali and Galilee suffered the same fate as the trans-jordanic tribes before Ephraim or Judah had been molested (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>). In the time of the Christian era this original disadvantage of their position was still felt; the speech of the Galileans "bewrayed them" by its uncouth pronunciation (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.73">Mt 26:73</reference>); and their distance from the seats of government and civilization at Jerusalem and Cæsarea gave them their character for turbulence or independence, according as it was viewed by their friends or their enemies. <div eID="gen25379" type="x-p"/>
entries.37c61398632f18fade0bb43c872f7c5c8ad3ac7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13341"/><div sID="gen25380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13341"/><hi type="bold">16. The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up--</hi>The prophetic strain to which these words belong commences with the seventh chapter of Isaiah, to which the sixth chapter is introductory, and goes down to the end of the twelfth chapter, which hymns the spirit of that whole strain of prophecy. It belongs to the reign of Ahaz and turns upon the combined efforts of the two neighboring kingdoms of Syria and Israel to crush Judah. In these critical circumstances Judah and her king were, by their ungodliness, provoking the Lord to sell them into the hands of their enemies. What, then, is the burden of this prophetic strain, on to the passage here quoted? First, Judah shall not, cannot perish, because Immanuel, the Virgin's Son, is to come forth from his loins. Next, one of the invaders shall soon perish, and the kingdoms of neither be enlarged. Further, while the Lord will be the Sanctuary of such as confide in these promises and await their fulfilment, He will drive to confusion, darkness, and despair the vast multitude of the nation who despised His oracles, and, in their anxiety and distress, betook themselves to the lying oracles of the heathen. This carries us down to the end of the eighth chapter. At the opening of the ninth chapter a sudden light is seen breaking in upon one particular part of the country, the part which was to suffer most in these wars and devastations--"the land of Zebulun, and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee and the Gentiles." The rest of the prophecy stretches over both the Assyrian and the Chaldean captivities and terminates in the glorious Messianic prophecy of the eleventh chapter and the choral hymn of the twelfth chapter. Well, this is the point seized on by our Evangelist. By Messiah's taking up His abode in those very regions of Galilee, and shedding His glorious light upon them, this prediction, He says, of the Evangelical prophet was now fulfilled; and if it was not thus fulfilled, we may confidently affirm it was not fulfilled in any age of the Jewish ceremony, and has received no fulfilment at all. Even the most rationalistic critics have difficulty in explaining it in any other way. <div eID="gen25380" type="x-p"/>
entries.81632cd65adfe6e48fdd1ecf740a3943c6c2ca1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13342"/><div sID="gen25381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13342"/><hi type="bold">17. From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent; for the kingdom of heaven is at hand--</hi>Thus did our Lord not only take up the strain, but give forth the identical summons of His honored forerunner. Our Lord sometimes speaks of the new kingdom as already come--in His own Person and ministry; but the economy of it was only "at hand" until the blood of the cross was shed, and the Spirit on the day of Pentecost opened the fountain for sin and for uncleanness to the world at large.<div eID="gen25381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25382" type="x-p"/> Calling of Peter and Andrew James and John (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.18-Matt.4.22">Mt 4:18-22</reference>). <div eID="gen25382" type="x-p"/>
entries.48a46a904fe142ba1dac6258a85396b6cdbcfe1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13343"/><div sID="gen25383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13343"/><hi type="bold">18. And Jesus, walking--</hi>The word "Jesus" here appears not to belong to the text, but to have been introduced from those portions of it which were transcribed to be used as church lessons; where it was naturally introduced as a connecting word at the commencement of a lesson.<div eID="gen25383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the Sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishers--</hi>"called Peter" for the reason mentioned in <reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>. <div eID="gen25384" type="x-p"/>
entries.169db158017e889da791f7b4d732cdcb65fbf87f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13344"/><div sID="gen25385" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13344"/><hi type="bold">19. And he saith unto them, Follow me--</hi>rather, as the same expression is rendered in Mark, "Come ye after Me" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.17">Mr 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen25385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and I will make you fishers of men--</hi>raising them from a lower to a higher fishing, as David was from a lower to a higher feeding (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.70-Ps.78.72">Psa 78:70-72</reference>). <div eID="gen25386" type="x-p"/>
entries.051f25ee3dd8af85760c47b729d633a002b1071f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13345"/><div sID="gen25387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13345"/>20. And they straightway left their nets, and followed him. <div eID="gen25387" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d9d43d9617a741630aa4278aa8279c42d034ab2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13346"/><div sID="gen25388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13346"/><hi type="bold">21. And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship--</hi>rather, "in the ship," their fishing boat.<div eID="gen25388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25389" type="x-p"/> with Zebedee their father, mending their nets: and he called them. <div eID="gen25389" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe005c1b2c56ae16c65299e6962b286bde265b63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13347"/><div sID="gen25390" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13347"/><hi type="bold">22. And they immediately left the ship and their father--</hi>Mark adds an important clause: "They left their father Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.20">Mr 1:20</reference>); showing that the family were in easy circumstances.<div eID="gen25390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and followed him--</hi>Two harmonistic questions here arise: First, Was this the same calling as that recorded in <reference osisRef="John.1.35-John.1.42">Joh 1:35-42</reference>? Clearly not. For, (1) That call was given while Jesus was yet in Judea: this, after His return to Galilee. (2) Here, Christ calls Andrew: there, Andrew solicits an interview with Christ. (3) Here, Andrew and Peter are called together: there, Andrew having been called, with an unnamed disciple, who was clearly the beloved disciple (see on <reference osisRef="John.1.40">Joh 1:40</reference>), goes and fetches Peter his brother to Christ, who then calls him. (4) Here, John is called along with James his brother: there, John is called along with Andrew, after having at their own request had an interview with Jesus; no mention being made of James, whose call, if it then took place, would not likely have been passed over by his own brother. Thus far nearly all are agreed. But on the next question opinion is divided: <hi type="bold">Was this the same calling as that recorded in <reference osisRef="Luke.5.1-Luke.5.11">Lu 5:1-11</reference>? Many able critics think so. But the following considerations are to us decisive against it. First here, the four are called separately, in pairs: in Luke, all together. Next, in Luke, after a glorious miracle: here, the one pair are casting their net, the other are mending theirs. Further, here, our Lord had made no public appearance in Galilee, and so had gathered none around Him; He is walking solitary by the shores of the lake when He accosts the two pairs of fishermen: in Luke, the multitude are pressing upon Him, and hearing the word of God, as He stands by the Lake of Gennesaret--</hi>a state of things implying a somewhat advanced stage of His early ministry, and some popular enthusiasm. Regarding these successive callings, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.5.1">Lu 5:1</reference>.<div eID="gen25391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25392" type="x-p"/> First Galilean Circuit (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.23-Matt.4.25">Mt 4:23-25</reference>). <div eID="gen25392" type="x-p"/>
entries.74de4c8ed67f6f0f45c3912c2027eaadf53f7547: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13348"/><div sID="gen25393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13348"/><hi type="bold">23. And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues--</hi>These were houses of local worship. It cannot be proved that they existed before the Babylonish captivity; but as they began to be erected soon after it, probably the idea was suggested by the religious inconveniences to which the captives had been subjected. In our Lord's time, the rule was to have one wherever ten learned men or professed students of the law resided; and they extended to Syria, Asia Minor, Greece, and most places of the dispersion. The larger towns had several, and in Jerusalem the number approached five hundred. In point of officers and mode of worship, the Christian congregations are modelled after the synagogue.<div eID="gen25393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and preaching the gospel of the kingdom--</hi>proclaiming the glad tidings of the kingdom,<div eID="gen25394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and healing all manner of sickness--</hi>every disease.<div eID="gen25395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and all manner of disease among the people--</hi>every complaint. The word means any incipient malady causing "softness." <div eID="gen25396" type="x-p"/>
entries.966aeadd905b1313fc303a8017b22654e9cc8a1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13349"/><div sID="gen25397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13349"/><hi type="bold">24. And his fame went throughout all Syria--</hi>reaching first to the part of it adjacent to Galilee, called Syro-Phoenicia (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.26">Mr 7:26</reference>), and thence extending far and wide.<div eID="gen25397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they brought unto him all sick people--</hi>all that were ailing or unwell. Those<div eID="gen25398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that were taken--</hi>for this is a distinct class, not an explanation of the "unwell" class, as our translators understood it.<div eID="gen25399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with divers diseases and torments--</hi>that is, acute disorders.<div eID="gen25400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and those which were possessed with devils--</hi>that were demonized or possessed with demons.<div eID="gen25401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and those which were lunatic--</hi>moon-struck.<div eID="gen25402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and those that had the palsy--</hi>paralytics, a word not naturalized when our version was made.<div eID="gen25403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he healed them--</hi>These healings were at once His credentials and illustrations of "the glad tidings" which He proclaimed. After reading this account of our Lord's first preaching tour, can we wonder at what follows? <div eID="gen25404" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a751d1cd1de72ab0acb71d6fd21c33e68518052: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13350"/><div sID="gen25405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13350"/><hi type="bold">25. And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and from Decapolis--</hi>a region lying to the east of the Jordan, so called as containing ten cities, founded and chiefly inhabited by Greek settlers.<div eID="gen25405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and from Jerusalem, and from beyond Jordan--</hi>meaning from Perea. Thus not only was all Palestine upheaved, but all the adjacent regions. But the more immediate object for which this is here mentioned is, to give the reader some idea both of the vast concourse and of the varied complexion of eager attendants upon the great Preacher, to whom the astonishing discourse of the next three chapters was addressed. On the importance which our Lord Himself attached to this first preaching circuit, and the preparation which He made for it, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.1.35-Mark.1.39">Mr 1:35-39</reference>. CHAPTERS 5-8<div eID="gen25406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25407" type="x-p"/> Sermon on the Mount.<div eID="gen25407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">That this is the same Discourse as that in <reference osisRef="Luke.6.17-Luke.6.49">Lu 6:17-49</reference>--</hi>only reported more fully by Matthew, and less fully, as well as with considerable variation, by Luke--is the opinion of many very able critics (of the Greek commentators; of Calvin, Grotius, Maldonatus--Who stands almost alone among Romish commentators; and of most moderns, as Tholuck, Meyer, De Wette, Tischendorf, Stier, Wieseler, Robinson). The prevailing opinion of these critics is that Luke's is the original form of the discourse, to which Matthew has added a number of sayings, uttered on other occasions, in order to give at one view the great outlines of our Lord's ethical teaching. But that they are two distinct discourses--the one delivered about the close of His first missionary tour, and the other after a second such tour and the solemn choice of the Twelve--is the judgment of others who have given much attention to such matters (of most Romish commentators, including Erasmus; and among the moderns, of Lange, Greswell, Birks, Webster and Wilkinson. The question is left undecided by Alford). Augustine's opinion--that they were both delivered on one occasion, Matthew's on the mountain, and to the disciples; Luke's in the plain, and to the promiscuous multitude--is so clumsy and artificial as hardly to deserve notice. To us the weight of argument appears to lie with those who think them two separate discourses. It seems hard to conceive that Matthew should have put this discourse before his own calling, if it was not uttered till long after, and was spoken in his own hearing as one of the newly chosen Twelve. Add to this, that Matthew introduces his discourse amidst very definite markings of time, which fix it to our Lord's first preaching tour; while that of Luke, which is expressly said to have been delivered immediately after the choice of the Twelve, could not have been spoken till long after the time noted by Matthew. It is hard, too, to see how either discourse can well be regarded as the expansion or contraction of the other.
